passage: Parul, you hid behind the door when Mama Uncle came for a hug. Come here; let your Nirmala Nani tell you something. When I was nine, there was a big uncle in our family who always said, “Come, give your uncle a kiss!” and pulled us onto his lap. I hated it. My stomach went tight every time his car came. One day I told my mother. She didn't laugh. She said, “You never have to kiss or hug anyone. Offer a namaste, and I'll stand beside you.” At the next visit, I pressed my palms together. He frowned, but my mother said, “That's her greeting.” That goes for everyone, Parul. Even for me.

qa.q: What did the uncle always say?
qa.a: He always said, “Come, give your uncle a kiss!”

qa.q: What was young Nirmala feeling when the uncle's car came?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and full of dread, her stomach going tight because she hated being pulled onto his lap and kissed.

qa.q: What choice did Nirmala's mother make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She listened, said Nirmala never had to kiss or hug anyone, offered a namaste instead and stood beside her, backing her up in front of the uncle.

qa.q: How did the uncle react to the namaste?
qa.a: He frowned, probably surprised or put out, but her mother made clear it was her greeting.

grounding: Shows a child's right to decline a hug or kiss from anyone and offer another greeting, with an adult backing that choice.

passage: Arrivals at the airport were packed and noisy, and the car was waiting in a no-parking zone, so everyone was rushing. Samir's cousin Mehak burst through the crowd with her arms wide. “Samir! Hug!” Samir froze. He liked Mehak, but hugs made him feel squashed and stiff. Behind her, his aunt was already saying, “Quick, quick, the car!” No time to explain. Samir held out his fist instead, grinning. “Fist bump? Our secret greeting?” Mehak paused, arms still open, then laughed and bumped his fist hard. “Secret greeting!” she said, and grabbed a suitcase handle instead. They ran for the car together.

qa.q: Where was the car waiting?
qa.a: The car was waiting in a no-parking zone.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when Mehak ran at him with open arms?
qa.a: Samir felt awkward and uncomfortable, liking Mehak but disliking the squashed feeling of hugs.

qa.q: Why was the fist bump a good choice in the rush?
qa.a: It was quick, warm and fun, letting Samir decline the hug without hurting Mehak or holding everyone up.

qa.q: How did Mehak take the offered fist bump?
qa.a: Mehak paused but then laughed and enjoyed the “secret greeting”, still feeling welcomed 😊

grounding: Shows a child choosing a fist bump instead of a hug based on comfort, and the greeting still carrying warmth.

passage: On Manoj Sir's last day at their school in Lucknow, the whole class lined up to say goodbye. Most kids flung their arms round him; a few shook his hand; one boy high-fived him so hard it echoed. Jyoti stood near the back, twisting her card in her hands. She wanted to say goodbye properly, but hugging a teacher felt strange to her. When her turn came, Manoj Sir crouched a little and held up both options: one hand for a handshake, one palm for a high-five. “Your choice, Jyoti.” She took the handshake and gave him the card. He read it and smiled. “This means a lot.”

qa.q: What did Jyoti give Manoj Sir?
qa.a: Jyoti gave him her card.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as she twisted her card at the back?
qa.a: Jyoti felt unsure and a bit uncomfortable, wanting to say a proper goodbye but not wanting to hug a teacher.

qa.q: How did Manoj Sir make it easy for Jyoti?
qa.a: He held up both a handshake and a high-five and said it was her choice, so she could say goodbye in a way she felt comfortable with.

qa.q: How might Manoj Sir feel about the different goodbyes?
qa.a: He probably valued every one, the hugs, the handshakes and Jyoti's card, as signs the class cared.

grounding: Shows a child choosing a handshake over a hug based on comfort, and an adult offering the choice.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: Monday. Ujjwal's diary. A new girl came today: Salma, from Hyderabad. Ma'am put her next to me. I wanted to say hello, but my mouth wouldn't work. I get like that with new people. So I smiled and pushed my extra pencil towards her, the good one with the eraser. She smiled back. At lunch she sat alone, and I couldn't make myself walk over. So I waved from my table and pointed at the empty chair next to me. She came! We didn't talk much. She showed me her tiffin, and I showed her mine. Tomorrow I'm going to try saying one full sentence.

qa.q: Where did Salma come from?
qa.a: Salma came from Hyderabad.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when the words wouldn't come?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt shy and a little frustrated, wanting to welcome Salma but finding it hard to talk to new people.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal welcome Salma without many words?
qa.a: Ujjwal smiled, shared the good pencil and waved Salma over to the empty chair at lunch.

qa.q: What might Salma have felt when Ujjwal pointed to the chair?
qa.a: Salma probably felt relieved and welcomed, no longer eating alone on her first day.

grounding: Shows a shy child welcoming a new classmate with a smile, a shared pencil and a wave to an empty seat.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: When the new boy, Nitin, climbed off the tractor-trolley at the village school gate, clutching a city schoolbag, Uday was the first to walk up. “Namaste. I'm Uday. You're in our class.” Nitin nodded, eyes darting. Uday showed him everything: where to leave his chappals outside the classroom, the handpump that squeaks, the neem tree where they eat, and which step is broken. At lunch he tipped half his roasted chana into Nitin's hand. “My Aai makes it spicy. Tell me if it's too much.” Nitin ate a handful, coughed, laughed and asked for more.

qa.q: What did Uday tip into Nitin's hand?
qa.a: Uday tipped half his roasted chana into Nitin's hand.

qa.q: What was Nitin likely feeling when he arrived with darting eyes?
qa.a: Nitin was likely nervous and unsure in a new place, far from the city school he knew.

qa.q: Which of Uday's actions made Nitin feel included?
qa.a: Greeting him first, showing him practical things like the chappals and the broken step, and sharing his chana at lunch.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had walked up to Nitin at the gate?
qa.a: Nitin might have spent his first day alone and confused, not knowing the rules or where to eat.

grounding: Shows a child welcoming a new classmate with a hello, a tour and a shared snack, teaching inclusion.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: When Zeynep arrived in Rosa's class in Berlin, she spoke almost no German. She stood by the door holding her new timetable upside down. Rosa jumped up. “Hallo! I'm Rosa!” Zeynep looked blank. Rosa pointed to herself: “Rosa.” Then to Zeynep, eyebrows raised. “Zeynep,” she whispered. Rosa grinned, turned the timetable the right way up and pointed to the empty seat beside her. At break, Rosa offered half her apple and showed her the toilets, the water fountain and the good swing. By the afternoon, Zeynep had taught her merhaba, and Rosa said it every time they passed in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Zeynep holding upside down?
qa.a: Zeynep was holding her new timetable upside down.

qa.q: What was Zeynep likely feeling at the door?
qa.a: Zeynep was likely nervous and lost, speaking almost no German in a new school.

qa.q: How did Rosa welcome Zeynep across the language gap?
qa.a: She used names and gestures, fixed the timetable, offered a seat and half her apple, and showed her the important places.

qa.q: What did learning merhaba show about the friendship?
qa.a: It showed the welcome went both ways, with Zeynep sharing her language and Rosa using it warmly.

grounding: Shows a child welcoming a new student who speaks another language with a seat, a snack and a tour.

passage: At the school library's reading-buddy hour, Harsha was helping a small Class 2 girl with a book about frogs. She pointed at a word. “What's a habitat?” Harsha puffed up. “It's a home for animals.” The girl frowned. “So a frog has a house?” Madhuri Ma'am, shelving books nearby, looked over. “Good start, Harsha. How could you explain it so she can picture it?” Harsha thought. “It's the kind of place an animal needs to live. Frogs need water and plants and bugs to eat. So a pond is a frog's habitat. Your house has a kitchen and a bed; a pond has what a frog needs.” The girl nodded hard.

qa.q: What was the book about?
qa.a: The book was about frogs.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when first explaining?
qa.a: Harsha felt confident and proud at first, and then challenged when the girl was still confused.

qa.q: How did Madhuri Ma'am's question help Harsha explain better?
qa.a: Asking how to help her picture it pushed Harsha to add details and a comparison, making the definition clearer.

qa.q: What did the first explanation make the small girl think?
qa.a: It made her think a frog lives in a house, so she was confused until the pond comparison.

grounding: Shows a child defining a word to show understanding, and a how question pushing the explanation deeper.

passage: I'm Irawati, and on Friday Naveen had to explain kho-kho to the visiting students from Japan. At first it was a mess. “So you sit, and someone runs, and you say kho, and then you can't go that way, but the other one can…” The visitors looked at each other. One of them asked, “Why can the chaser only go one direction?” Naveen stopped. He thought for a second, then said, “So the runners have a chance. Otherwise it's too easy.” After that he explained more slowly: who sits, who chases, why the kho. He used his hands. By the second game they were shouting kho louder than us. I don't know how he felt, but he looked taller.

qa.q: Where were the visiting students from?
qa.a: The visiting students were from Japan.

qa.q: What might Naveen have felt when the visitors looked at each other?
qa.a: Naveen probably felt flustered and unsure, realising his explanation was muddled.

qa.q: How did the visitor's question improve Naveen's explanation?
qa.a: Asking why made Naveen explain the reason behind the rule, which helped him explain the whole game more clearly.

qa.q: How does Irawati describe the change in Naveen?
qa.a: Irawati saw his explanation go from a mess to clear, and noticed he looked taller afterwards.

grounding: Shows a child explaining the rules of a game, and a why question helping the explanation grow clearer.

passage: Monday: Sarika read out her civics homework: “Democracy is a system of government by the people.” Her brother Thomas looked up from his phone. “What does that mean, though?” Sarika opened her mouth and shut it. “It's… what the book says.” Wednesday: Sarika tried again at dinner. “It's like our class monitor vote. Everyone gets one vote, and the one with the most wins. And if they're bad, we can vote for someone else next time.” Thomas nodded. “Why does that matter?” “So one person can't just decide everything forever.” Saturday: Their Ammachi asked what she was studying. Sarika explained democracy using the monitor vote. Ammachi said, “Now I understand it better too.”

qa.q: What example did Sarika use to explain democracy?
qa.a: Sarika used their class monitor vote.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she opened her mouth and shut it on Monday?
qa.a: Sarika felt stuck and a little embarrassed, realising she could repeat the definition but not explain it.

qa.q: How did Thomas's questions help Sarika?
qa.a: Asking what it meant and why it mattered pushed Sarika from reciting the book to explaining it in her own words with an example.

qa.q: What did Ammachi gain from Sarika's explanation?
qa.a: Ammachi said she understood democracy better too, showing how clear Sarika's explanation had become.

grounding: Shows a child's definition growing clearer over several days as why and how questions push for depth.

passage: In the hill village school, Hafsa Teacher asked Tenzin to tell the class the story his grandfather had told him about the lost yak. Tenzin started, and went on, and on: the snow, the prayer flags, his grandfather's boots, the other yaks, what they had for dinner. After five minutes the class was fidgeting. Hafsa Teacher raised a hand. “It's a lovely story. Can you give it to us in three lines? Who, what went wrong, how it ended.” Tenzin frowned, counting on his fingers. “A yak got lost in the snow. Grandfather followed its bell for a whole night. He found it sheltering by the monastery wall.” The class clapped.

qa.q: Where did Grandfather find the yak?
qa.a: He found it sheltering by the monastery wall.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling as he counted on his fingers?
qa.a: Tenzin was concentrating hard and maybe a little unsure, working out which parts of the long story mattered most.

qa.q: How did Hafsa Teacher help Tenzin summarise?
qa.a: She praised the story and gave a simple frame, who, what went wrong and how it ended, to pick out the key points.

qa.q: What was the long version like for the class?
qa.a: The class grew restless and fidgety, losing the thread in all the extra details.

grounding: Shows a child learning to summarise a long story in three lines, with an adult modelling how to choose key points.

passage: Mr Anders Lund had spent ten minutes explaining the water cycle to his class in Oslo, drawing arrows all over the board until it looked like spaghetti. He stopped and laughed. “I've made that very confusing, haven't I? Sorry. Who can help me say it in three steps?” Clara looked at the mess of arrows and felt her brain untangle it. She put up her hand. “Water goes up as vapour. It makes clouds. It comes down as rain.” Mr Lund wiped the board clean and wrote her three lines. “That's clearer than I was. Thank you, Clara.” Clara felt her cheeks go warm.

qa.q: How long had Mr Lund spent explaining?
qa.a: He had spent ten minutes explaining the water cycle.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling when Mr Lund thanked her?
qa.a: Clara felt pleased and a little shy, her cheeks going warm at the praise.

qa.q: What did Mr Lund model for the class?
qa.a: He modelled admitting that his explanation was confusing and then choosing a few key points to make it clear.

qa.q: How might the class have felt before Clara's summary?
qa.a: The class was probably confused by the spaghetti of arrows and relieved when it became three simple steps.

grounding: Shows an adult admitting a muddled explanation and a child summarising it in a few key points.

passage: At the hostel's Sunday meeting, the warden explained new rules about phone time, laundry days and the study room. Amandeep had been at the doctor and missed it. At dinner he asked Vishal, “What did I miss?” Vishal waved his fork. “Loads. Phones something, laundry changed, and the study room, um, closes, or opens…” Amandeep looked more confused. Vishal stopped. “Wait. Let me do it properly.” He counted on his fingers. “One: phones only after dinner. Two: laundry is Wednesday now, not Monday. Three: the study room stays open till ten.” Then he added, “The laundry bit I'm not sure about. Let's check the notice board.” It said Wednesday.

qa.q: What day is laundry now?
qa.a: Laundry is on Wednesday now, not Monday.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he stopped and said “Wait”?
qa.a: Vishal felt a little embarrassed at the muddled first answer and determined to get it right for Amandeep.

qa.q: What did Vishal do well the second time?
qa.a: He picked out three key points, counted them clearly, and admitted which one he wasn't sure about so they could check.

qa.q: Why was Amandeep relying on Vishal?
qa.a: Amandeep had missed the meeting because he was at the doctor, so he needed a clear summary.

grounding: Shows a child clarifying a muddled summary by choosing key points and admitting what was not clear.

passage: In the flooded paddy field, Tanuja Maushi was showing Yogesh how to plant rice seedlings. He pushed the first bunch into the mud and looked up. “Like this? Is this right?” Five seedlings later: “This one? Is it deep enough?” A neighbour on the bund laughed. “That boy has no confidence!” Tanuja didn't think so. He was watching her hands carefully and copying them. She answered each time with something exact: “Good, but two fingers deeper.” “Spacing is right, a hand apart.” By the end of the row, Yogesh was asking less and planting faster. “You checked, so you learned,” she told him.

qa.q: How far apart should the seedlings be?
qa.a: The seedlings should be a hand apart.

qa.q: What was Yogesh likely feeling as he kept asking “Is this right?”
qa.a: Yogesh was keen and a bit unsure, wanting to get it right while learning something new.

qa.q: How did Tanuja answer Yogesh's checks?
qa.a: She answered each question with an exact tip, such as two fingers deeper or a hand apart, treating his checking as effort to learn.

qa.q: How did the neighbour on the bund read Yogesh's questions?
qa.a: The neighbour read the questions as a lack of confidence, not as careful learning.

grounding: Shows an adult reading a child's repeated is this right as effort to learn and answering with specifics.

passage: Before the relay at the Johannesburg school's sports day, Coach Thabo gave the team their instructions. “Hold the baton at the bottom. Run on the inside of the lane. Pass it from your right hand into their left.” Tariq repeated it under his breath, then out loud. “Bottom, inside, right to left. Right, Coach?” A teammate rolled his eyes. “He always does that.” Coach Thabo crouched. “That's good. Repeating it back is how you make sure. One fix: the next runner starts moving before you reach them, not after.” Tariq nodded and said it again. His hand-off that afternoon was the cleanest of the day.

qa.q: Which hand should the baton be passed from?
qa.a: The baton should be passed from the right hand into the next runner's left.

qa.q: What was Tariq feeling as he repeated the instructions?
qa.a: Tariq was focused and a little anxious to get the hand-off right.

qa.q: How did Coach Thabo respond to Tariq's repeating back?
qa.a: He praised it as a way of making sure and added one specific fix about when the next runner should start.

qa.q: How did the teammate who rolled his eyes see Tariq's habit?
qa.a: The teammate saw it as annoying, not as a smart way to learn.

grounding: Shows an adult treating a child's repeating back of instructions as effort to learn and answering with a specific fix.

passage: At the community centre's pottery class, Lavanya lifted her little bowl off the wheel and held it up. “Is it right, Dilnaz Aunty?” She had asked after every step: after centring the clay, after opening the hole, after pulling up the walls. Another parent in the room murmured, “She's so unsure of herself.” Dilnaz Aunty didn't think so. She turned the bowl slowly in her hands. “The base is even, well done. The rim is thick on this side; next time press gently with your thumb here.” Lavanya watched her thumb. “Like this?” She tried it on a scrap of clay. “Exactly,” said Dilnaz Aunty.

qa.q: Where was the pottery class?
qa.a: The pottery class was at the community centre.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling as she held up her bowl?
qa.a: Lavanya felt hopeful and eager to learn, wanting to know if she had got each step right.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz Aunty's answer help Lavanya learn?
qa.a: She gave specific feedback, praising the even base and showing exactly how to fix the thick rim.

qa.q: How did the other parent read Lavanya's questions?
qa.a: The other parent saw them as a sign of being unsure of herself, not as effort to learn.

grounding: Shows an adult reading a child's did I do it right as effort to learn and answering with specifics.

passage: In the school van crawling through Kolkata traffic, Abhinav sat by the window, not joining the usual fight about songs. He didn't laugh when the driver honked at a cow. Kalyani, beside him, nudged his arm. “Are you okay? You're so quiet.” He shrugged. “Fine. Don't want to talk.” Kalyani nodded and didn't push. She pulled out her chocolate bar and put a piece on his knee. They rode in silence. When the van stopped at his lane, he said, without looking at her, “My dog's sick. The vet's coming today.” Kalyani squeezed his hand. “Tell me tomorrow how he is.”

qa.q: What did Kalyani put on Abhinav's knee?
qa.a: She put a piece of her chocolate bar on his knee.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling as he sat quietly by the window?
qa.a: Abhinav was worried and sad about his sick dog, and not ready to talk about it yet.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that made it easier for Abhinav to share?
qa.a: She asked kindly, then accepted his no, stayed beside him and offered chocolate without pushing.

qa.q: What would change if Kalyani had kept asking?
qa.a: Abhinav might have closed off completely and not shared the news about his dog at all.

grounding: Shows a child asking a quiet friend are you okay, and the friend not wanting to answer at first.

passage: “Hey. Are you okay?” Sangeeta sat on the step beside Lalremsiami, who had stared at her shoes since the bell. “Mm.” “You didn't eat lunch.” “Wasn't hungry.” Sangeeta waited. “You don't have to tell me. I just noticed.” Lalremsiami picked at her shoelace. “Someone said Mizo food smells weird. I don't want to talk about it more.” “Okay. That was a horrible thing to say. Can we just tell Ma'am, together, before the bus? You don't have to explain much.” A long pause. “Okay.” In the staff room, Ma'am listened and said, “Thank you for telling me. That's not okay, and it's not your fault.” Then she went to find the class before the last bell.

qa.q: What had someone said to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Someone said Mizo food smells weird.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she stared at her shoes?
qa.a: She was hurt and upset by the unkind comment about her food, and didn't want to talk much about it.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta balance asking and not pushing?
qa.a: She asked gently, said Lalremsiami didn't have to tell her, accepted the short answer and offered to go to Ma'am together that same day.

qa.q: How did Ma'am respond when they told her?
qa.a: Ma'am thanked them, said it wasn't okay and wasn't Lalremsiami's fault, and went to speak to the class before the last bell.

grounding: Shows a child kindly asking a quiet friend are you okay, the friend only partly answering, and a trusted adult acting the same day.

passage: I'm Pankaj. Last month, after Dhruv lost the chess final, he sat on the bench outside the hall with his hood up. I went over and asked, “Are you okay?” He snapped, “Obviously not. Go away.” I felt stung. I almost said something mean back. Instead I said, “Okay. I'll be at the canteen,” and walked off. I kept thinking I'd done it wrong. The next morning Dhruv came and sat next to me at assembly. “Sorry about yesterday,” he said. “I just needed to not talk.” Then he told me about the move he'd missed. Now I know asking is still right, even when the answer is no.

qa.q: What did Dhruv lose?
qa.a: Dhruv lost the chess final.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when Dhruv snapped?
qa.a: Pankaj felt stung and hurt, and briefly wanted to say something mean back.

qa.q: Why was Pankaj's reply after the snap a good choice?
qa.a: Saying where to find Pankaj and then leaving gave Dhruv space while keeping the door open.

qa.q: What did Dhruv need right after the final?
qa.a: Dhruv was upset about losing and needed time not to talk before he was ready to share.

grounding: Shows a child asking a friend are you okay after a loss, and the friend not wanting to answer yet.

passage: At breakfast in the hill-station hostel, Harish announced, “I saw a leopard last night, near the water tank!” The table groaned. Dolma raised an eyebrow. “You're joking. You said you saw a ghost last week.” Harish's face fell. “I'm not joking this time.” Dolma thought about it. Suspicious, yes, but a leopard near a hill hostel wasn't impossible. “Okay. Let's ask the night guard.” After breakfast they found him at the gate. He nodded seriously. “Yes, it came by at two. I've told the warden.” That evening the warden announced that no one was to go near the tank after dark. Dolma turned to Harish. “Sorry. I should have checked first.”

qa.q: Where did Harish say he saw the leopard?
qa.a: Harish said he saw it near the water tank.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when the table groaned and Dolma doubted him?
qa.a: Harish felt hurt and frustrated at not being believed, especially since it was true this time.

qa.q: What did Dolma do with her suspicion that was wise?
qa.a: She treated her doubt as a reason to check facts, asking the night guard, instead of deciding Harish was lying.

qa.q: Why did Dolma doubt Harish at first?
qa.a: Harish had claimed to see a ghost the week before, so his new story sounded like another joke.

grounding: Shows a child voicing doubt about a story and treating suspicion as a cue to check facts, not a verdict.

passage: I'm Charu. On Tuesday, Mihir burst into class saying, “The zoo trip's cancelled! Sir told me!” Everyone groaned. Sunaina, next to me, narrowed her eyes. “Hmm. Yesterday you told us the canteen was closing forever.” Mihir went red. “This is true!” I thought Sunaina would just call him a liar. She didn't. She said, “Maybe. Let's ask Sir before we believe it.” At break she went to the staff room, and I tagged along. Sir said, “Not cancelled. Postponed by a week because of the rain.” So Mihir was half right. Sunaina told him, “You were close. Sorry I doubted you.” I don't know if she believed him before, but she checked.

qa.q: Why was the zoo trip postponed?
qa.a: It was postponed by a week because of the rain.

qa.q: What might Mihir have felt when Sunaina narrowed her eyes?
qa.a: Mihir probably felt embarrassed and defensive, knowing his canteen story had been wrong.

qa.q: How did Sunaina use her suspicion well?
qa.a: She treated it as a reason to check with Sir rather than calling Mihir a liar, and apologised when he turned out half right.

qa.q: How did Charu expect Sunaina to react?
qa.a: Charu expected Sunaina to call Mihir a liar, and was surprised she checked instead.

grounding: Shows a child's suspicion about a classmate's news being used as a cue to check facts rather than a verdict on his character.

passage: Monday: Ganga spotted a purple gel pen on Yogesh's desk, exactly like the ones in her set. “Where did you get that?” “Found it,” her brother mumbled. Found it? That doesn't add up, she thought. She almost shouted “Thief!” Tuesday: Instead, she counted her own set. Twelve pens. None missing. Still, the story felt odd. Thursday: At dinner, Amma said, “Yogesh, did you tell your sister I bought you the same pens? He was too shy to say he wanted ones like yours.” Yogesh went pink. Ganga laughed. “You could have just said!” She was glad she had counted before she called him anything.

qa.q: How many pens were in Ganga's set?
qa.a: There were twelve pens in Ganga's set.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he mumbled “Found it”?
qa.a: Yogesh was shy and a bit embarrassed to admit he wanted pens just like his sister's.

qa.q: What did Ganga do with her suspicion that helped?
qa.a: She counted her own pens to check the facts before accusing, which stopped her calling Yogesh a thief.

qa.q: Why did Amma explain at dinner?
qa.a: Amma knew the truth and could see Yogesh was too shy to say he had wanted pens like Ganga's.

grounding: Shows a child's suspicion when a story doesn't add up, and checking facts instead of reaching a verdict about her brother.

passage: In Binita Aunty's tuition room above the chemist in Bhopal, she finished explaining long division and asked, “Everyone got it?” Tejas nodded fast with the others. “Yes, got it.” Then she gave them a sum. Tejas stared at it. He didn't know where to start. His ears went hot. Everyone else was writing. He could copy from the boy next to him. Instead he put up his hand. “Binita Aunty, I said I got it, but I don't. I'm not sure what to do after the first step.” A couple of kids smirked. Binita Aunty didn't. “Thank you for saying so. That's the most useful sentence anyone's said today. Come, let's do the second step together.”

qa.q: Where was Binita Aunty's tuition room?
qa.a: It was above the chemist in Bhopal.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he stared at the sum?
qa.a: Tejas felt embarrassed and anxious, realising he had said he understood when he didn't.

qa.q: Why was Tejas's choice to put up his hand a strength?
qa.a: Admitting the gap honestly got him real help, instead of copying and staying confused.

qa.q: How did Binita Aunty respond to Tejas's admission?
qa.a: She thanked him, called it the most useful sentence of the day and helped him with the second step.

grounding: Shows a child matching confidence to knowledge by admitting a gap, and a supportive teacher rewarding it.

passage: “Harsha, what's the capital of Australia?” “Sydney, obviously.” Kavitha Ma'am tilted her head. “Are you sure, or are you guessing?” “Sure. It's the biggest.” “Hmm. How sure, out of ten?” Harsha paused. “Nine.” “What would make it a ten?” Harsha frowned. “If I… checked?” “Go on, then.” Harsha flipped to the atlas page. His face fell. “Canberra.” “So what's the honest number now?” “For Sydney, zero,” Harsha said, and the class laughed, and so did he. “Next time I'll say ‘I think’ when I'm guessing.” “That,” said Kavitha Ma'am, “is exactly how scientists talk.”

qa.q: What does the atlas show is the capital of Australia?
qa.a: The atlas shows that the capital is Canberra.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when his face fell?
qa.a: Harsha felt surprised and a bit embarrassed to find his confident answer was wrong.

qa.q: How did Kavitha Ma'am help Harsha match his confidence to his knowledge?
qa.a: She asked how sure he was out of ten and what would make it a ten, which led him to check and to plan to say “I think” when guessing.

qa.q: How did Kavitha Ma'am feel about Harsha's final plan?
qa.a: She was pleased, saying that “I think” when guessing is exactly how scientists talk.

grounding: Shows a child learning to match confidence to knowledge, with a teacher rewarding honest uncertainty.

passage: I'm Siddharth. When I joined the under-twelve football team, Coach Naveen asked if I understood the offside rule. I said, “Yes, Coach,” because everyone else was nodding and I didn't want to look stupid. In the first match I got caught offside four times. The other team's players laughed. After the game I finally told Coach, “I didn't really understand it. I just said I did.” I thought he'd be angry. Instead he said, “That's braver than scoring.” He showed me with bottle caps on the bench until I got it. Now when I'm not sure, I say so first. It saves a lot of running.

qa.q: How many times was Siddharth caught offside in the first match?
qa.a: Siddharth was caught offside four times.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when saying “Yes, Coach” at the start?
qa.a: Siddharth felt worried about looking stupid while everyone else nodded, so pretended to understand.

qa.q: What did Coach Naveen do that made admitting the gap feel safe?
qa.a: He praised the admission as braver than scoring and patiently explained the rule with bottle caps.

qa.q: How did the other team's players react to the offside calls?
qa.a: They laughed at Siddharth for being caught offside again and again.

grounding: Shows a child learning that admitting a gap and asking for help is a strength a supportive coach rewards.

passage: Wednesday. Irfan's diary. Today Disha and I argued at lunch about whether a spider is an insect. I said yes, obviously, it's a creepy-crawly. She said no, insects have six legs and spiders have eight. I got louder. She got the science book out and showed me. Eight legs. Two body parts, not three. My face went hot, and I wanted to say the book was old. But I said, “Okay. You're right. Spiders aren't insects.” Then I added, “But they're still creepy-crawlies.” She laughed and said, “Yes, fine, that's true.” At home Abbu said conceding like that is harder than winning. It didn't feel like losing, actually.

qa.q: How many legs does a spider have, according to the book?
qa.a: According to the book, spiders have eight legs.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when the book proved Disha right?
qa.a: Irfan felt embarrassed, face hot, and was tempted to argue the book was old.

qa.q: What did Irfan's “okay, you're right… but” achieve?
qa.a: It conceded the fact gracefully while keeping a fair point, so the argument ended with both of them laughing.

qa.q: How did Disha respond to Irfan's concession?
qa.a: Disha laughed and agreed spiders are still creepy-crawlies, meeting Irfan halfway.

grounding: Shows a child conceding a point gracefully and qualifying it, and an adult praising it so it doesn't feel like losing.

passage: On the dusty path to the Tuesday haat, Ritu and Sarika argued about which way was shorter. “Along the canal is quicker,” said Sarika. “No, through the mustard fields,” said Ritu. They raced, one each way. Sarika was already at the bangle stall, grinning, when Ritu arrived, panting. Ritu wanted to say Sarika had cheated. Instead she wiped her face and said, “Okay, the canal is shorter. But the field way has shade, and I'm not melting like you.” Sarika looked at her own red face and laughed. “Fair. Canal to come, fields to go back?” Ritu's grandmother, bargaining for onions nearby, nodded. “Well argued, both of you.”

qa.q: Where was Sarika when Ritu arrived?
qa.a: Sarika was already at the bangle stall.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she arrived panting?
qa.a: Ritu felt disappointed at losing and briefly tempted to accuse Sarika of cheating.

qa.q: How did Ritu's “Okay, but” turn the argument into a plan?
qa.a: By conceding the canal was shorter and adding that the fields have shade, she kept her point and led to a fair plan for both paths.

qa.q: How did Ritu's grandmother view the argument?
qa.a: She approved, saying both girls argued well, since they settled it fairly.

grounding: Shows a child conceding a point with okay, you're right and qualifying with but, and an adult praising the graceful concession.

passage: In their group project in a Vancouver classroom, Dalia and Mei couldn't agree on the poster layout. Dalia wanted the title at the bottom, big and bold. Mei wanted it at the top. “Nobody reads the bottom first,” Mei said. Dalia opened her mouth to argue, then looked at the other groups' posters on the wall. Every title was at the top, and she had read them first. “Okay,” she said slowly. “You're right about the top.” Then she added, “But can it be in my dark green? It stands out more.” Mei held the green pen up against the paper. “Yes. It does.” Their teacher, passing, said, “That's what good teamwork sounds like.”

qa.q: What colour did Dalia want the title in?
qa.a: Dalia wanted it in her dark green.

qa.q: What was Dalia feeling as she looked at the other posters?
qa.a: Dalia felt a little reluctant at first, then convinced as she saw every title at the top.

qa.q: Why did the teacher praise the way they settled it?
qa.a: Dalia conceded gracefully and added a fair qualification, so both ideas made the poster better without anyone feeling they lost.

qa.q: How did Mei respond to Dalia's suggestion about colour?
qa.a: Mei tested the green pen against the paper and agreed it stood out more.

grounding: Shows a child conceding a point and qualifying it with a yes, but, and an adult praising graceful conceding.

passage: In the school library in Guwahati, the book club had to choose one book for the term. Jaya slapped a thick fantasy novel on the table. “This one. It's the best book ever written. Anyone who disagrees is wrong.” Lalremsiami felt her face heat. She had wanted the mystery, and part of her wanted to shout, “That's so boring!” Instead she took a breath. “I see it differently. It's six hundred pages, and some of us read slowly. Could we do the mystery now and yours next term?” Jaya frowned, then flipped through the fat book. “Six hundred and twelve,” she admitted. “Okay. Mystery first, then mine.” They shook on it.

qa.q: How many pages did the fantasy novel have?
qa.a: It had six hundred and twelve pages.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when Jaya said anyone who disagrees is wrong?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt annoyed and tempted to shout that the book was boring.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami disagree respectfully?
qa.a: She took a breath, said she saw it differently, gave a reason about the length and slow readers, and offered a fair compromise.

qa.q: What changed Jaya's mind?
qa.a: Jaya checked the page count herself and saw Lalremsiami's point, so she agreed to read the mystery first.

grounding: Shows a child saying I see it differently with a reason instead of shouting, and disagreement not rejecting the person.

passage: “Bruno should sleep inside from now on,” said Kiran. “No way,” said Sachin. “He'll chew the sofa. That's stupid.” Kiran's jaw tightened. “Don't call it stupid.” “Sorry. It's not stupid. I just disagree.” “Why, though?” “Because last time he chewed Papa's chappal and got locked out all day. Outside, he's got his kennel.” Kiran thought. “I see that. But it's winter now, and he shivers at night.” Sachin paused. “Okay, that's fair. What if he sleeps on the veranda with a blanket? Warm, but no sofa.” Kiran grinned. “Deal. I still think inside is nicer, though.” “You're allowed to think that.”

qa.q: What did Bruno chew last time?
qa.a: Bruno chewed Papa's chappal.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when Sachin called the idea stupid?
qa.a: Kiran felt hurt and irritated, jaw tightening at having the idea dismissed.

qa.q: What did Sachin change that kept the talk respectful?
qa.a: Sachin apologised for “stupid”, said he just disagreed, gave his reason and then suggested a middle way.

qa.q: What reason did Kiran give that changed Sachin's mind?
qa.a: Kiran pointed out that it's winter and Bruno shivers at night, which Sachin agreed was fair.

grounding: Shows children learning to say I disagree, and here's why, instead of insulting, so disagreement is not rejection of the person.

passage: I'm Salma. Last year in history, Sumit Sir said the Taj Mahal was built in ten years. I'd read it took more like twenty. My heart was pounding; you don't argue with Sumit Sir. Before, I'd have just sulked. This time I put up my hand. “Sir, I think I see it differently. The book in the library says around twenty years, because the gardens and buildings around it took longer.” The class went silent. Sir looked at me for a long moment, then smiled. “You're right that the whole complex took longer. Good disagreeing, Salma. Bring me that book.” I did. He read from it the next day.

qa.q: How long did the library book say the Taj Mahal took to build?
qa.a: The library book said around twenty years.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling before putting up a hand?
qa.a: Salma felt nervous, heart pounding, because arguing with Sumit Sir felt risky.

qa.q: How did Salma disagree respectfully?
qa.a: Salma said “I think I see it differently” and gave a reason with a source, instead of sulking or accusing Sir of being wrong.

qa.q: How did Sumit Sir respond to being disagreed with?
qa.a: He listened, agreed the whole complex took longer, praised the good disagreeing and asked to see the book.

grounding: Shows a child disagreeing with a teacher by saying I see it differently and giving a reason, instead of sulking.
